label: def:moderate_net
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:moderate_net}
	A net \((w_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon\in(0,1]}\) of finite words over
	a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) is \emph{moderate} if there exist
	\(N\in\mathbb{N}\), \(C>0\), and \(\varepsilon_0>0\) such that
	\[
	|w_\varepsilon|\le C\varepsilon^{-N}
	\qquad(\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0).
	\]
	The set of moderate nets is denoted by \(\mathcal{E}_M(\Sigma^*)\).
head: environment
name: Moderate net

label: def:log_equiv
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:log_equiv}
	Two moderate nets \((u_\varepsilon)\) and \((v_\varepsilon)\) are
	\emph{logarithmically equivalent}, written
	\((u_\varepsilon)\sim(v_\varepsilon)\), if for every
	\(m\in\mathbb{N}\) there exists \(\varepsilon_0>0\) such that
	\[
	\min\{\operatorname{lcp}(u_\varepsilon,v_\varepsilon),
	\operatorname{lcs}(u_\varepsilon,v_\varepsilon)\}
	\ge
	m\log_2(1/\varepsilon)
	\qquad(\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0),
	\]
	where \(\operatorname{lcp}\) and \(\operatorname{lcs}\) denote the longest common prefix and
	suffix, respectively.
head: environment
name: Asymptotic equivalence

title: Remark
body_md:
Two moderate nets are logarithmically equivalent when they agree on
	their first and last \(m\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\) letters, for every
	fixed \(m\), as \(\varepsilon\to0^+\).  This is a strong condition:
	it forces the two nets to have the same asymptotic prefix and suffix
	profile on logarithmic scales, while allowing arbitrary behaviour in
	the middle.  The quotient \(\widetilde{\Sigma}^*\) therefore retains
	exactly the information that is visible to logarithmic-prefix
	functionals.
head: environment
name: Intuition

label: def:log_prefix_functional
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:log_prefix_functional}
	A \emph{logarithmic-prefix functional} is a family of maps
	\(F_\varepsilon:\Sigma^*\to\mathbb{C}\) such that:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item \emph{Prefix dependence:} for each \(\varepsilon\), the value
		\(F_\varepsilon(w)\) depends only on the prefix of \(w\) of
		length \(N_0(\varepsilon)+1\), where
		\[
		N_0(\varepsilon)=\lfloor\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\rfloor.
		\]
		\item \emph{Moderate growth:} there exist \(C>0\) and \(M\in\mathbb{N}\)
		such that
		\[
		|F_\varepsilon(w)|\le C\,(1+|w|)^M
		\qquad(\varepsilon\in(0,1],\;w\in\Sigma^*).
		\]
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Logarithmic-prefix functional

label: lem:invariance
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:invariance}
	Let \(F_\varepsilon\) be a logarithmic-prefix functional.  If
	\((u_\varepsilon)\) and \((v_\varepsilon)\) are moderate nets with
	\((u_\varepsilon)\sim(v_\varepsilon)\), then
	\[
	F_\varepsilon(u_\varepsilon)=F_\varepsilon(v_\varepsilon)
	\qquad\text{eventually.}
	\]
	Consequently, \(F_\varepsilon\) induces a well-defined map
	\[
	\widetilde{F}:\widetilde{\Sigma}^*\longrightarrow\widetilde{\mathbb{C}}
	\]
	on the asymptotic monoid.
head: environment
name: Invariance

title: Remark
body_md:
The image \(\widetilde{\mathbb{C}}\) denotes the ring of asymptotic complex
	numbers, that is, equivalence classes of nets of complex numbers
	modulo the relation of eventual agreement on logarithmic scales.  In
	practice, when the limit
	\[
	\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{w})=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}F_\varepsilon(w_\varepsilon)
	\]
	exists in \(\mathbb{C}\) for some (hence every) representative
	\((w_\varepsilon)\) of \(\mathbf{w}\in\widetilde{\Sigma}^*\), we identify
	\(\widetilde{F}(\mathbf{w})\) with its limit.
head: environment

label: def:eval_functional
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:eval_functional}
	Let \(P=\prod_{n\ge1}q_n^{a(n)}\) be a divergent product with sign
	sequence \((a(n))\subset\mathbb{C}\), and let
	\[
	\Lambda_k=\sum_{n=1}^{k}a(n)\log q_n
	\]
	denote its prefix functional.  The \emph{weighted evaluation
		functional} associated with \(P\) is the logarithmic-prefix
	functional
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:eval_general}
		\mathcal{F}_\varepsilon(u)
		=
		\sum_{k=2}^{N_0(\varepsilon)}
		\frac{\Lambda(u[1\ldots k])}{k^{\alpha}},
		\qquad
		u\in\Sigma^*,
	\end{equation}
	where \(N_0(\varepsilon)=\lfloor\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\rfloor\) and
	the exponent \(\alpha>0\) is chosen according to the heuristic
	\(\alpha=\sigma_1+1\), with \(\sigma_1\) the abscissa of absolute
	convergence of the associated Dirichlet series.
head: environment
name: Weighted evaluation functional

label: rem:choice_alpha
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:choice_alpha}
	The heuristic \(\alpha=\sigma_1+1\) ensures that the summands
	\(\Lambda_k/k^{\alpha}\) decay fast enough for \(\mathcal{F}_\varepsilon\) to
	converge as \(\varepsilon\to0^+\), while remaining faithful to the
	divergence type of the product.  In the case of a product associated
	with a bounded sign sequence, one has \(\sigma_1=1\), hence
	\(\alpha=2\).  This is precisely the value used in
	Section~\ref{sec:encoding} for the product \(P_\omega\).
head: environment
name: Choice of the exponent \(\alpha\

label: def:regularized_value
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:regularized_value}
	Let \(P=\prod_{n\ge1}q_n^{a(n)}\) be a divergent product, and let
	\(\mathcal{F}_\varepsilon\) be the weighted evaluation functional
	\eqref{eq:eval_general}.  Suppose that for some (hence every)
	canonical net \((w_\varepsilon)\) representing the sign sequence of
	\(P\) in \(\widetilde{\Sigma}^*\), the limit
	\[
	\mathcal{F}=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\mathcal{F}_\varepsilon(w_\varepsilon)
	\]
	exists in \(\mathbb{C}\).  The \emph{regularized value} of \(P\) is then
	defined as
	\[
	P_{\mathrm{ren}}=\exp(\mathcal{F}).
	\]
head: environment
name: Regularized value

title: Remark
body_md:
The construction above is purely asymptotic and algebraic.  It does
	not require the associated Dirichlet series to admit meromorphic
	continuation, nor does it invoke analytic continuation of any kind.
	This is the structural reason why the framework is applicable to
	products whose Dirichlet series have natural boundaries, such as the
	product \(P_\omega\) studied in this paper.
head: environment
name: Scope of the framework

label: thm:meretov
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:meretov}
	The function \(D_{\omega}(s)\) admits a meromorphic continuation
	to the half-plane \(\Re(s)>0\).  Its only possible singularity in
	this half-plane is at \(s=1\), where the simple pole of the factor
	\(\zeta(s)\) is cancelled by the simple zero of the local factor
	\(1-2^{1-s}\); hence \(s=1\) is a removable singularity of
	\(D_{\omega}\), and \(D_{\omega}\) is in fact analytic in
	\(\Re(s)>0\) after removal of this point.  The line
	\(\Re(s)=0\) is a \emph{natural boundary}: no analytic
	continuation across any arc of this line is possible.
head: environment
name: Meretov, 1987; Estermann--Dahlquist

label: cor:no_zeta
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:no_zeta}
	The derivative \(D_{\omega}'(0)\) does not exist.  Consequently,
	the product \(P_{\omega}\) cannot be regularized by zeta
	regularization or by any method requiring meromorphic continuation
	to \(s=0\).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The natural boundary at \(\Re(s)=0\) is a manifestation
	of the Estermann phenomenon: not every natural Dirichlet series
	admits a meromorphic continuation beyond its abscissa of
	convergence.  For \(D_{\omega}(s)\), the zeros of the local factors
	accumulate on the imaginary axis and create an impenetrable barrier.
	In particular, the identity
	\(D_{\omega}(s)=\prod_p(1-2p^{-s})/(1-p^{-s})\) for
	\(\Re(s)>1\) does \emph{not} extend beyond the abscissa of
	convergence, and cannot be used to define
	\(D_{\omega}(0)\).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The canonical net is not unique within its class
	\(\mathbf{w}_{\omega}\): any moderate net that agrees with
	\((w_\varepsilon)\) on the first and last
	\(m\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\) letters, for every \(m\), belongs to the
	same class.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:invariance}, the regularized value
	will be independent of this choice.
head: environment

label: rem:alpha_equal_two
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:alpha_equal_two}
	The exponent \(\alpha=2\) in \eqref{eq:Fomega} follows the heuristic
	\(\alpha=\sigma_1+1\) of Remark~\ref{rem:choice_alpha}, with
	\(\sigma_1=1\) the abscissa of absolute convergence of
	\(D_{\omega}(s)=\sum(-1)^{\omega(n)}n^{-s}\).  With this choice, the evaluation functional converges absolutely; the
	convergence is unconditional and follows from the classical zero-free
	region of \(\zeta(s)\); see Proposition~\ref{prop:convergence} below.
head: environment
name: Choice of the exponent \(\alpha=2\

label: prop:convergence
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:convergence}
	The series \(\mathcal{F}\) in \eqref{eq:F_def} converges absolutely.
	Consequently, the regularized value \(P_{\omega,\mathrm{ren}}\)
	is independent of the truncation scheme and of the ordering of the
	terms.
head: environment
name: Absolute convergence

title: Proof
body_md:
By the Estermann--Dahlquist theorem
	(Theorem~\ref{thm:estermann_dahlquist}), the Dirichlet series
	$D_{\omega}(s)$ admits a meromorphic continuation to the half-plane
	$\Re(s)>0$.  In this half-plane, the only possible singularity of
	$D_{\omega}(s)$ is at $s=1$, where the simple pole of $\zeta(s)$ is
	cancelled by the simple zero of the factor $1-2^{1-s}$ at $s=1$.
	Hence $D_{\omega}(s)$ is analytic in the half-plane $\Re(s)>0$ after
	removal of the point $s=1$.
	
	Since $D_{\omega}(s)$ is a Dirichlet series with bounded
	coefficients, absolutely convergent for $\Re(s)>1$ and analytic in a
	neighbourhood of the closed half-plane $\Re(s)\ge1$ (except for the
	removable point $s=1$, which is in fact a zero), the classical
	quantitative Perron--Tauberian theorem for multiplicative functions
	with bounded coefficients applies.  We refer to
	\cite[Chapter~II.5]{Tenenbaum2015} for the general statement of the
	theorem, and to \cite[Chapter~III.4]{Tenenbaum2015} for the
	derivation of the effective bound
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Tomega_effective}
		T_{\omega}(x)
		=
		\sum_{n\le x}(-1)^{\omega(n)}
		=
		O\!\left(x\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}\right)
	\end{equation}
	for some absolute constant $c>0$, valid unconditionally.  The key
	input is the classical zero-free region of $\zeta(s)$ (de la
	Vall\'ee Poussin, 1899), which enters through the standard
	explicit-formula argument.
	
	By Abel summation,
	\[
	\Lambda_k
	=
	T_{\omega}(k)\log k-\int_1^k T_{\omega}(t)\frac{dt}{t}.
	\]
	Substituting \eqref{eq:Tomega_effective} and using that
	\(\int_1^k e^{-c\sqrt{\log t}}\,dt\le k\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log k}}\)
	for \(k\ge2\), we obtain
	\[
	|\Lambda_k|
	\le
	C\,k\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log k}}\log k
	\]
	for some absolute constant \(C>0\).  Therefore
	\[
	\frac{|\Lambda_k|}{k^2}
	\le
	C\,\frac{e^{-c\sqrt{\log k}}\log k}{k}.
	\]
	The series
	\[
	\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-c\sqrt{\log k}}\log k}{k}
	\]
	converges: substituting \(u=\log k\), it is comparable to
	\[
	\int_{\log 2}^{\infty} e^{-c\sqrt{u}}\,u\,du<\infty.
	\]
	Hence \(\sum_{k\ge2}|\Lambda_k|/k^2<\infty\), and \(\mathcal{F}\)
	converges absolutely.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The absolute convergence of \(\mathcal{F}\) is a direct consequence of the
	effective zero-free region of \(\zeta(s)\), which is unconditional.
	In particular, no unproven hypothesis is required.  The vanishing
	of the first derivatives \(D_{\omega}(1)=D_{\omega}'(1)=0\) ensures
	that the principal terms cancel, and the residual series is
	absolutely summable thanks to the exponential decay of
	\(T_{\omega}(x)\).  This is a rigorous statement about the
	\emph{stability} of the regularization: the value
	\(P_{\omega,\mathrm{ren}}\) is invariant under reordering and
	truncation.
head: environment
name: Interpretation

title: Remark
body_md:
The monoid \(\widetilde{\Sigma}^*\) plays three essential roles:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item It provides a \emph{domain} on which the sign sequence
		\((-1)^{\omega(n)}\) can be encoded as a single algebraic
		object \(\mathbf{w}_{\omega}\), despite being an infinite
		word.
		\item It guarantees that the evaluation functional
		\(\mathcal{F}_\varepsilon\) is \emph{well defined} on this object,
		via the invariance lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:invariance}).
		\item It makes the regularized value \emph{canonical}: the
		value \(P_{\omega,\mathrm{ren}}\) depends only on the class
		\(\mathbf{w}_{\omega}\), not on the particular net
		\((w_\varepsilon)\) chosen to represent it.
	\end{enumerate}
	Without the monoid, one could still compute the numerical value
	\(0.7731\) by summing the series, but one could not assert that
	this value is intrinsic to the sign sequence \((-1)^{\omega(n)}\)
	rather than an artifact of the truncation.
head: environment
name: The role of the monoid

title: Remark
body_md:
The natural boundary of \(D_{\omega}(s)\) at \(\Re(s)=0\)
	(Theorem~\ref{thm:meretov}) is an obstruction to \emph{analytic
		continuation}.  The monoid framework does not attempt analytic
	continuation: it operates directly on the asymptotic prefix
	profile of the sign sequence, which is a purely combinatorial
	object.  The natural boundary is therefore irrelevant to the
	monoid construction.  This is the structural reason why the
	monoid succeeds where zeta regularization fails.
head: environment
name: Insensitivity to the natural boundary

label: lem:D_zero_order
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:D_zero_order}
	The Dirichlet series \(D_{\omega}(s)\) satisfies
	\[
	D_{\omega}(1)=0,
	\qquad
	D_{\omega}'(1)=0.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For \(\Re(s)>1\), the Euler product is
	\[
	D_{\omega}(s)
	=
	\prod_{p}\frac{1-2p^{-s}}{1-p^{-s}}.
	\]
	Isolate the prime \(p=2\):
	\[
	D_{\omega}(s)=f(s)H(s),
	\]
	where
	\[
	f(s)=\frac{1-2^{1-s}}{1-2^{-s}},
	\qquad
	H(s)=\prod_{p\ge 3}\frac{1-2p^{-s}}{1-p^{-s}}.
	\]
	At \(s=1\), we have \(f(1)=0\), and a direct computation gives
	\(f'(1)=2\ln 2\).
	
	We now prove that \(H(1)=0\).  Rewrite \(H(s)\) as
	\[
	H(s)
	=
	\prod_{p\ge 3}(1-2p^{-s})
	\;\cdot\;
	\prod_{p\ge 3}\frac{1}{1-p^{-s}}
	=
	A(s)\,\frac{1-2^{-s}}{\zeta(s)},
	\]
	where
	\[
	A(s)=\prod_{p\ge 3}(1-2p^{-s})
	\]
	is analytic for \(\Re(s)>0\) (with zeros but no poles), and we used
	the factorization
	\[
	\prod_{p\ge 3}\frac{1}{1-p^{-s}}
	=
	(1-2^{-s})\zeta(s).
	\]
	Since \(\zeta(s)\) has a simple pole at \(s=1\), the factor
	\((1-2^{-s})/\zeta(s)\) has a simple zero there.  On the other
	hand, from
	\[
	\log A(s)
	=
	\sum_{p\ge 3}\log(1-2p^{-s})
	=
	-2\sum_{p\ge 3}p^{-s}+O(1)
	\]
	and the standard estimate
	\(\sum_{p\ge 3}p^{-s}=\log\zeta(s)+O(1)\) as \(s\to1\), we obtain
	\[
	\log A(s)
	=
	-2\log\zeta(s)+O(1)
	=
	2\log(s-1)+O(1),
	\]
	so \(A\) has a zero of order \(2\) at \(s=1\).  Since the factor
	\((1-2^{-s})/\zeta(s)\) has a simple zero there, the product
	\(H(s)\) is analytic in a neighbourhood of \(s=1\), and satisfies
	\(H(1)=0\).  Moreover, \(H'(1)\) exists.
	
	Therefore
	\[
	D_{\omega}(1)=f(1)H(1)=0,
	\]
	and, since \(f(1)=0\) and \(H(1)=0\),
	\[
	D_{\omega}'(1)
	=
	f'(1)H(1)+f(1)H'(1)
	=
	0.
	\]
	This proves the claim.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The vanishing of \(D_{\omega}(1)\) and \(D_{\omega}'(1)\) is the
	analytic counterpart of the fact that the leading term in the
	asymptotic expansion of the log-partial sums vanishes.  It is also
	the reason why the leading contribution to the evaluation
	functional \(\mathcal{F}\) cancels: the cancellation responsible for
	\(D_{\omega}'(1)=0\) is encoded in the alternating sign sequence,
	while the residual series is absolutely summable by
	Proposition~\ref{prop:convergence}.
head: environment

label: prop:D_second_derivative
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We keep the notation of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:D_zero_order}.
	We have \(D_{\omega}(s)=f(s)H(s)\), with
	\[
	f(s)=\frac{1-2^{1-s}}{1-2^{-s}},
	\qquad
	H(s)=\prod_{p\ge 3}\frac{1-2p^{-s}}{1-p^{-s}}.
	\]
	Since \(f(1)=0\) and \(H(1)=0\) (the latter was proved in
	Lemma~\ref{lem:D_zero_order}), the Leibniz rule gives
	\[
	D_{\omega}''(1)
	=
	f''(1)H(1)+2f'(1)H'(1)+f(1)H''(1)
	=
	2f'(1)H'(1).
	\]
	We have already computed \(f'(1)=2\ln 2\).  It remains to compute
	\(H'(1)\).
	
	Write
	\[
	H(s)=\frac{G(s)}{\zeta(s)(1-2^{-s})},
	\]
	where
	\[
	G(s)
	=
	\prod_{p\ge 3}\frac{1-2p^{-s}}{(1-p^{-s})^2}
	=
	\prod_{p\ge 3}\frac{p^s(p^s-2)}{(p^s-1)^2}.
	\]
	The product \(G(s)\) converges absolutely for \(\Re(s)>1/2\).  At
	\(s=1\),
	\[
	G(1)
	=
	\prod_{p\ge 3}\frac{p(p-2)}{(p-1)^2}
	=
	C_2.
	\]
	Since \(\zeta(s)\) has a simple pole at \(s=1\) with residue \(1\),
	we have
	\[
	\frac{1}{\zeta(s)}=(s-1)+O\bigl((s-1)^2\bigr).
	\]
	Also \(1-2^{-s}\to 1/2\) as \(s\to 1\).  Hence
	\[
	H(s)
	=
	2C_2(s-1)+O\bigl((s-1)^2\bigr),
	\]
	so \(H(1)=0\) and
	\[
	H'(1)=2C_2.
	\]
	Substituting into the expression for \(D_{\omega}''(1)\), we obtain
	\[
	D_{\omega}''(1)
	=
	2\cdot(2\ln 2)\cdot(2C_2)
	=
	8C_2\ln 2.
	\]
	This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: rem:correction
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:correction}
	Some preliminary notes contained the value \(2C_2\ln 2\) for
	\(D_{\omega}''(1)\).  That value is incorrect.  The correct value is
	\(8C_2\ln 2\), as proved above.  The error arose from an
	incomplete treatment of the factor \((1-2^{-s})^{-1}\) in the
	expression for \(H(s)\).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The appearance of the twin prime constant \(C_2\) in the second
	derivative is not accidental.  The local factor of \(D_{\omega}(s)\)
	at an odd prime \(p\) is
	\[
	\frac{1-2p^{-s}}{1-p^{-s}}
	=
	1-\frac{p^{-s}}{1-p^{-s}}
	=
	1-p^{-s}-p^{-2s}-p^{-3s}-\cdots
	\]
	The coefficient of \(p^{-s}\) is \(-1\), which is the same as the
	coefficient of \(p^{-s}\) in the Euler product of
	\(\zeta(s)^{-1}\).  The second-order correlations between distinct
	primes are therefore governed by the same combinatorial structure
	that produces the twin prime constant.  This is a manifestation of
	the fact that \((-1)^{\omega(n)}\) is a multiplicative function
	whose local factors are rational functions with a zero at
	\(p^{-s}=1/2\).
head: environment
name: Arithmetic interpretation

label: cor:F_anchor
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:F_anchor}
	The evaluation functional \(\mathcal{F}\) satisfies
	\[
	\mathcal{F}
	=
	-D_{\omega}'(1)
	+
	O(1)
	=
	O(1),
	\]
	and the leading non-trivial term in the expansion of
	\(D_{\omega}(s)\) near \(s=1\) is
	\[
	\frac{1}{2}D_{\omega}''(1)(s-1)^2
	=
	4C_2\ln 2\,(s-1)^2.
	\]
	No quantitative identity linking \(\mathcal{F}\) to
	\(D_{\omega}''(1)\) is claimed.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first assertion follows from the decomposition
	\eqref{eq:F_transparent} and the fact that \(D_{\omega}'(1)=0\).
	The second assertion is the Taylor expansion of \(D_{\omega}(s)\)
	at \(s=1\), using Lemma~\ref{lem:D_zero_order} and
	Proposition~\ref{prop:D_second_derivative}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Corollary~\ref{cor:F_anchor} explains why the numerical computation
	of \(\mathcal{F}\) in Section~\ref{sec:numerical} converges to a finite
	value: the leading divergence is cancelled by the vanishing of
	\(D_{\omega}(1)\) and \(D_{\omega}'(1)\), and the residual series
	is absolutely summable by Proposition~\ref{prop:convergence}.  The
	vanishing of the first derivatives is of the same arithmetic origin
	as the companion identity
	\(D_{\omega}''(1)=8C_2\ln 2\), although no quantitative relation
	between \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(D_{\omega}''(1)\) is established.
head: environment

label: rem:oscillation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:oscillation}
	The pronounced oscillation of the early partial sums (for instance,
	\(\mathcal{F}(10^4)=+0.0424\)) reflects the slow initial decay of the
	summands \(\Lambda_k/k^2\): although the series converges
	absolutely, the effective bound
	\(|\Lambda_k|/k^2=O(e^{-c\sqrt{\log k}}\log k/k)\) is dominated by
	the prefactor \(\Lambda_K/K\) for moderate values of \(K\), so the
	partial sums exhibit large fluctuations before settling down.  The
	stabilization observed for \(K\ge 5\times10^6\) is consistent with
	the theoretical prediction of Proposition~\ref{prop:convergence}.
head: environment

label: prop:error_analysis
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Error analysis

title: Proof
body_md:
By exchanging the order of summation in \eqref{eq:F_K},
	\[
	\mathcal{F}(K)
	=
	\sum_{n=1}^{K}(-1)^{\omega(n)}\log n
	\sum_{k=\max(2,n)}^{K}\frac{1}{k^2}.
	\]
	On the other hand, by definition of the trigamma function,
	\[
	\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{Tri}}(K)
	=
	\sum_{n=1}^{K}(-1)^{\omega(n)}\log n
	\sum_{k=\max(2,n)}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k^2}.
	\]
	Subtracting, we obtain
	\[
	\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{Tri}}(K)-\mathcal{F}(K)
	=
	\sum_{n=1}^{K}(-1)^{\omega(n)}\log n
	\sum_{k=K+1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k^2}
	=
	\Lambda_K
	\sum_{k=K+1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k^2}.
	\]
	Using the standard asymptotic expansion
	\[
	\sum_{k=K+1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k^2}
	=
	\frac{1}{K}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{K^2}\right),
	\]
	we obtain
	\[
	\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{Tri}}(K)-\mathcal{F}(K)
	=
	\frac{\Lambda_K}{K}
	+
	O\!\left(\frac{|\Lambda_K|}{K^2}\right).
	\]
	
	It remains to bound \(|\Lambda_K|\).  By the effective bound
	\eqref{eq:Tomega_effective} and Abel summation,
	\[
	|\Lambda_K|
	\le
	C'\,K\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log K}}\log K
	\]
	for absolute constants \(C',c>0\).  Substituting into the
	expression above gives
	\[
	\bigl|\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{Tri}}(K)-\mathcal{F}(K)\bigr|
	\le
	C\,\frac{e^{-c\sqrt{\log K}}\log K}{K},
	\]
	which is the claimed bound \eqref{eq:error_bound}.
	
	Finally, to justify the statement on the decay rate: for
	\(0<\alpha\le1\), the ratio
	\[
	\frac{e^{-c\sqrt{\log K}}\log K/K}{K^{-\alpha}}
	=
	K^{\alpha-1}\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log K}}\log K
	\]
	tends to \(0\) as \(K\to\infty\), because the exponential factor
	\(e^{-c\sqrt{\log K}}\) decays faster than any power of
	\(\log K\), while \(K^{\alpha-1}\to0\) or \(K^{\alpha-1}=1\) for
	\(\alpha<1\) or \(\alpha=1\), respectively.  For \(\alpha>1\),
	the ratio equals \(K^{\alpha-1}e^{-c\sqrt{\log K}}\log K\), which
	tends to \(+\infty\) since \(K^{\alpha-1}\) grows polynomially
	while the exponential factor is only subpolynomial.  This proves
	the stated range of validity.
head: environment

label: rem:num_check
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:num_check}
	At \(K=10^7\), the observed difference between the two methods is
	of order \(1.68\times10^{-3}\).  The theoretical bound
	\eqref{eq:error_bound} involves the implicit constant \(c\) of the
	de la Vall\'ee Poussin zero-free region, which is not explicit in
	the literature; for the range of \(K\) considered, the discrepancy
	is dominated by the prefactor \(\Lambda_K/K\).  The observed value
	is fully consistent with the bound, and the agreement between the
	two methods provides an independent numerical verification that
	the value \(\mathcal{F}\approx-0.2573\) is not an artifact of truncation
	or floating-point accumulation.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The value \(P_{\omega,\mathrm{ren}}\approx 0.7731\) is a new
	constant of arithmetic origin.  It cannot be obtained by zeta
	regularization (Theorem~\ref{thm:meretov}), nor by any method
	requiring meromorphic continuation to \(s=0\); it is obtained
	instead by the canonical prescription of the monoid framework.
	Its existence and well-definedness are guaranteed by
	Proposition~\ref{prop:convergence} and the axioms of \cite{C1}.
	The companion analytical identity
	\(D_{\omega}''(1)=8C_2\ln 2\)
	(Proposition~\ref{prop:D_second_derivative}) shows that the same
	arithmetic structure that governs the regularized value also
	governs the local curvature of \(D_\omega(s)\) at \(s=1\).  No
	quantitative identity linking the two constants is claimed.
head: environment
name: A new arithmetic constant

label: thm:estermann_dahlquist
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:estermann_dahlquist}
	Let \(h\) be as above.  Then:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item The Euler product \(D_h(s)\) admits a meromorphic
		continuation to the half-plane \(\Re(s)>0\).  Its poles in
		this half-plane are contained in the set of points \(s\) such
		that \(h(p^{-s})\) has a pole for some prime \(p\)
		(cancellations between different local factors may occur).
		Its zeros in this half-plane include the points \(s\) such
		that \(h(p^{-s})\) vanishes for some prime \(p\) and no
		other local factor has a pole at the same point \(s\).
		\item If \(h\) is a product of cyclotomic polynomials (up to a
		non-vanishing analytic factor), then \(D_h(s)\) extends
		meromorphically to the whole complex plane.
		\item Conversely, if \(h\) is \emph{not} a product of
		cyclotomic polynomials, then the line \(\Re(s)=0\) is a
		natural boundary for \(D_h(s)\): no analytic continuation
		across any arc of this line is possible.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Estermann, 1928; Dahlquist, 1952

title: Remark
body_md:
The dichotomy in Theorem~\ref{thm:estermann_dahlquist} is the
	content of the Estermann--Dahlquist theory.  The key point is that
	a zero of \(h\) at a point \(z_0\in\overline{\mathbb{D}}\) that is not a
	root of unity produces a family of zeros of the local factors
	\(h(p^{-s})\) which accumulate on the line \(\Re(s)=0\) and
	cannot be cancelled by the poles of other factors.  This prevents
	the meromorphic continuation beyond \(\Re(s)=0\).  We make the
	mechanism explicit in
	Subsection~\ref{subsec:accumulation_appendix} below.
head: environment

label: lem:h_analytic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:h_analytic}
	The function
	\[
	h(z)=\frac{1-2z}{1-z}
	\]
	is analytic in the open unit disk \(\mathbb{D}\), has a simple
	pole at \(z=1\) on the unit circle, and has a simple zero at
	\(z=1/2\) inside \(\mathbb{D}\).  Its Taylor coefficients at
	\(z=0\) are rational integers.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Writing
	\[
	h(z)=\frac{1-2z}{1-z}
	=
	(1-2z)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}z^{k}
	=
	1-\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}z^{k},
	\]
	we see that \(h\) is a rational function with a simple pole at
	\(z=1\) and a simple zero at \(z=1/2\).  The Taylor coefficients
	are \(h(0)=1\) and \(h^{(k)}(0)/k!=-1\) for all \(k\ge1\), which
	are rational integers.
head: environment

label: lem:h_not_cyclotomic
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A product of cyclotomic polynomials is a polynomial whose zeros
	are all roots of unity.  But \(h\) has a zero at \(z=1/2\), which
	is not a root of unity.  Hence \(h\) cannot be a product of
	cyclotomic polynomials.  Equivalently, the only cyclotomic factor
	of \(h\) is \(1-z\), which corresponds to the pole at \(z=1\); the
	zero at \(z=1/2\) has no cyclotomic interpretation.
head: environment

label: thm:natural_boundary_appendix
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:natural_boundary_appendix}
	The Dirichlet series
	\[
	D_{\omega}(s)
	=
	\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{\omega(n)}}{n^{s}}
	=
	\prod_{p}\frac{1-2p^{-s}}{1-p^{-s}},
	\qquad
	\Re(s)>1,
	\]
	admits a meromorphic continuation to the half-plane
	\(\Re(s)>0\).  In this half-plane, the only possible singularity
	of \(D_{\omega}(s)\) is at \(s=1\), where the simple pole of the
	factor \(\zeta(s)\) is cancelled by the simple zero of the local
	factor \(1-2^{1-s}\).  Consequently, \(s=1\) is a removable
	singularity of \(D_{\omega}\), and after removal of this point
	\(D_{\omega}\) is in fact analytic in \(\Re(s)>0\).  The line
	\(\Re(s)=0\) is a natural boundary: no analytic continuation
	across any arc of this line is possible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Euler product representation
	\[
	D_{\omega}(s)=\prod_{p}h(p^{-s}),
	\qquad
	h(z)=\frac{1-2z}{1-z},
	\]
	is valid for \(\Re(s)>1\).  By Lemma~\ref{lem:h_analytic}, the
	function \(h\) satisfies the hypotheses of
	Theorem~\ref{thm:estermann_dahlquist}.  By
	Lemma~\ref{lem:h_not_cyclotomic}, \(h\) is not a product of
	cyclotomic polynomials.  Therefore, applying
	Theorem~\ref{thm:estermann_dahlquist}:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item \(D_{\omega}(s)\) admits a meromorphic continuation to
		\(\Re(s)>0\).  The poles of the local factors \(h(p^{-s})\)
		occur at \(p^{-s}=1\), that is, at \(s=2\pi i k/\log p\)
		for \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\).  All these points lie on the
		boundary \(\Re(s)=0\), so there is no pole of any local
		factor in the open half-plane \(\Re(s)>0\).  The factor
		\(\zeta(s)\), which arises when the product over primes is
		rewritten, has a simple pole at \(s=1\); this pole is
		cancelled by the simple zero of \(h(2^{-s})\) at \(s=1\),
		because \(h(2^{-1})=0\).  Hence \(D_{\omega}\) is analytic
		in \(\Re(s)>0\) after removal of the point \(s=1\).
		\item The line \(\Re(s)=0\) is a natural boundary for
		\(D_{\omega}(s)\).
	\end{enumerate}
	This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: cor:no_zeta_appendix
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:no_zeta_appendix}
	The derivative \(D_{\omega}'(0)\) does not exist.  Consequently,
	the product \(P_{\omega}=\prod_{n\ge1}n^{(-1)^{\omega(n)}}\) cannot
	be regularized by zeta regularization or by any method requiring
	meromorphic continuation to \(s=0\).
head: environment

label: lem:accumulation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:accumulation}
	For every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), there exists a sequence of primes
	\(p_{j}\to\infty\) and integers \(k_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}\) such that
	\[
	s_{p_{j},k_{j}}
	\longrightarrow
	it.
	\]
head: environment

label: eq:small_real_part
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix \(t\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).  Choose a prime
	\(p\) sufficiently large that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:small_real_part}
		\frac{\log 2}{\log p}<\varepsilon.
	\end{equation}
	Choose an integer \(k\) such that
	\[
	\left|\frac{2\pi k}{\log p}-t\right|
	<
	\frac{2\pi}{\log p}.
	\]
	Such an integer exists because the points
	\(2\pi k/\log p\), \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\), form a lattice of spacing
	\(2\pi/\log p\).  Then
	\[
	|s_{p,k}-it|
	\le
	\frac{\log 2}{\log p}
	+
	\frac{2\pi}{\log p}
	\longrightarrow 0
	\]
	as \(p\to\infty\).  Taking a sequence \(p_{j}\to\infty\) and
	adjusting \(k_{j}\) accordingly gives the result.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
It is important to distinguish two types of special points of
	\(D_\omega\) in the half-plane \(\Re(s)>0\):
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item \emph{Poles.}  These arise from poles of the local
		factors \(h(p^{-s})\).  For \(h(z)=(1-2z)/(1-z)\), the
		only pole is at \(z=1\), giving \(p^{-s}=1\), i.e.\
		\(s=2\pi i k/\log p\), \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\).  All these
		points lie on the imaginary axis \(\Re(s)=0\), except for
		\(k=0\), which gives \(s=0\).  Hence there are \emph{no}
		poles of \(D_\omega\) in the open half-plane
		\(\Re(s)>0\).
		\item \emph{Zeros.}  These arise from zeros of the local
		factors \(h(p^{-s})\) and are given by
		\eqref{eq:zeros_explicit}.  They form a dense subset of
		the imaginary axis as \(p\to\infty\), with real parts
		tending to \(0\).
	\end{enumerate}
	A zero of a meromorphic function is not a singularity: at a
	zero, the function is analytic and vanishes.  The natural
	boundary of \(D_\omega\) at \(\Re(s)=0\) is thus produced not by
	\emph{singularities} accumulating on the line, but by
	\emph{zeros} accumulating on it, which obstruct analytic
	continuation by the identity theorem.
head: environment
name: Poles versus zeros

title: Remark
body_md:
A naive argument would attempt to show the natural boundary by
	examining the expansion
	\[
	D_{\omega}(s)=\prod_{m\ge1}\zeta(ms)^{-c_{m}},
	\qquad
	c_{m}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{d\mid m}\mu\!\left(\frac{m}{d}\right)(2^{d}-1),
	\]
	and looking for poles at \(s=1/m\).  This fails for two reasons:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
		\item The factor \(\zeta(ms)^{-c_{m}}\) has a \emph{zero} at
		\(s=1/m\) (when \(c_{m}>0\)), not a pole, because
		\(\zeta(ms)\) has a pole there.
		\item The points \(1/m\) accumulate only at \(s=0\), not along
		the entire imaginary axis.
	\end{enumerate}
	The correct special points to examine are the zeros of the local
	factors \(h(p^{-s})\), given by \eqref{eq:zeros_explicit}, which
	do accumulate on the entire imaginary axis.
head: environment
name: Why the naive argument fails
